strengths: The method addresses a practical problem: adapting a pretrained model to an individual protein without additional homologs or experimental labels. It is simple and compatible with several existing protein models.

The evaluation spans fitness, structure, substrate classification, and subcellular localization, providing useful evidence that the approach transfers across different downstream heads and model sizes.

Structure prediction shows meaningful improvements on the selected challenging targets: ESMFold TM-score increases from 0.4649 to 0.5047, and ESM3 from 0.3480 to 0.3954. Comparisons against masked prediction and iterative decoding strengthen these results.

The authors construct a separate MaveDB validation dataset, explicitly avoid an ESMFold checkpoint with test-set leakage, report five-seed results, and provide substantial implementation and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach directly transfers established masked-modeling test-time training to proteins using standard SGD and LoRA. A compelling application contribution is possible, but the current evidence does not sufficiently establish its significance or distinguish it from straightforward single-sequence fine-tuning.

The headline fitness and function improvements are small. SaProt-650M increases from 0.4569 to 0.4583 Spearman, TPS mAP from 0.805 to 0.811, and localization accuracy from 0.627 to 0.634. Seed standard deviations measure optimization variability, not uncertainty across proteins or assays; paired confidence intervals are needed to establish robustness. The advertised '40% higher improvement' compares tiny leaderboard increments and overstates their practical importance.

The folding evaluation contains only 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. TPS evaluation also selects low-confidence examples. These are legitimate targeted settings, but full-dataset results and larger independent hard-target benchmarks are needed to establish applicability and quantify degradation. The ESMFold-based selection also leaves ESM3's evaluation scope unclear.

The perplexity argument does not explain why adaptation improves downstream prediction. Minimizing reconstruction loss on the same sequence can reflect memorization, and cross-protein correlations between perplexity and structure accuracy do not establish that reducing perplexity causes better representations. Figure 11 explicitly shows downstream performance deteriorating while perplexity continues decreasing. The claimed implication from perplexity minimization to improved generalization is therefore too strong.

Important controls are missing: adaptation to shuffled or unrelated sequences, component-wise update ablations, and comparisons with other adaptation strategies would help identify the source of improvement. Compute comparisons are also incomplete: ESM3 TTT takes approximately 20 seconds versus one second for the base model, while its CoT baseline uses eight decoding steps. Equal sampling counts for ESMFold do not account for TTT backward-pass costs.

Several protocol and reporting issues remain unresolved. TPS hyperparameter selection is not clearly separated from the cross-validation predictions used for reporting. Table 5 does not consistently support the claimed inverse relationship between gains and MSA depth; the largest ESM2 gains occur at medium depth. Appendix A.1.3 reverses the interpretation of the log-odds score's sign. Finally, code and dataset-generation resources are promised rather than supplied, limiting verification.

strengths: The method addresses a practical problem: adapting a pretrained protein model to an individual target without additional homologous sequences or target labels. The implementation is simple and broadly applicable.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning fitness, structure, and function prediction with several pretrained backbones. Folding improvements are promising: ESMFold's mean TM-score increases from 0.4649 to 0.5047, and ESM3's from 0.3480 to 0.3954 on the selected targets.

The authors construct a separate MaveDB validation dataset, use an ESMFold checkpoint chosen to avoid test-set leakage, report five-seed results, and provide hyperparameter sensitivity analyses. Masked prediction and iterative decoding are useful folding baselines.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the core procedure transfers existing masked-modeling test-time training to proteins using standard SGD and LoRA. This application could be valuable, but the current evidence and mechanistic analysis do not establish a sufficiently strong contribution for a top-tier conference.

The perplexity argument does not explain why adaptation should improve downstream predictions. Reducing reconstruction loss on the same sequence used for adaptation can reflect memorization; correlations measured across held-out proteins do not establish the benefit of this intervention. Figure 11 explicitly shows perplexity continuing to decrease while fitness prediction deteriorates. The manuscript acknowledges overfitting but does not reconcile it with the stronger explanatory claims in Section 3.3.

Several headline gains are very small. Both 650M fitness models improve average Spearman correlation by only 0.0014; TPS mAP improves by 0.006, and localization accuracy by 0.007. Seed standard deviations measure optimization variability, not uncertainty across proteins or assays. Paired confidence intervals over evaluation units are needed to establish how robust these gains are. The '40% higher improvement' framing exaggerates the practical significance of a tiny leaderboard increment.

The folding evaluation contains only 18 of 194 test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. These label-free filters are reasonable for targeting difficult cases, but the small, model-dependent subset limits generalization, particularly for ESM3. TPS evaluation similarly uses a confidence-filtered subset. Broader evaluation and sensitivity to selection thresholds are missing.

Compute efficiency and comparison fairness are incompletely established. ESM3 TTT uses 50 adaptation steps plus repeated structure decoding, whereas CoT uses eight decoding steps. Matching ESMFold prediction counts also does not match the additional backward-pass cost. The reported ESM3 runtime is approximately 20 seconds versus one second without TTT; broader runtime, memory, and matched-compute comparisons are needed.

The TPS hyperparameter-selection protocol is unclear: results aggregate predictions across five cross-validation folds, but the manuscript does not explain a separate or nested validation procedure for selecting TTT settings. Code and dataset-generation resources are promised rather than provided, limiting verification.

Some interpretations exceed the reported evidence. Table 5 does not consistently support preferential improvement at low MSA depth: ESM2 benefits most at medium depth, while SaProt 650M changes little across depth groups. Table 6 also reports unchanged SaProt 650M validation performance despite the claim that every method improves.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, broadly applicable approach to adapting protein models using only the target sequence, without requiring additional homologs or downstream labels. Its relevance to individual-protein research is well motivated.

The evaluation spans fitness, structure, and function prediction across several architectures and model sizes. Improvements across these different settings provide useful evidence that the approach transfers beyond a single task.

Structure prediction results are promising: ESMFold improves from 0.4649 to 0.5047 TM-score, and ESM3 from 0.3480 to 0.3954, outperforming the included masked-prediction and iterative-decoding baselines.

The authors construct a separate MaveDB validation dataset for fitness hyperparameter selection, explicitly avoid an ESMFold checkpoint with test-set overlap, and report multiple random seeds and substantial implementation details.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely transfers established masked-modeling test-time training to proteins using standard SGD and LoRA. The empirical contribution is therefore central, but its magnitude and generality are not yet sufficiently convincing for clear acceptance.

The headline fitness gains are small for the strongest models: both ESM2-650M and SaProt-650M improve by only 0.0014 average Spearman correlation. The claimed 40% larger leaderboard improvement emphasizes a relative comparison between very small increments. Function gains are similarly modest, including localization accuracy increasing from 0.627 to 0.634. Seed standard deviations do not establish uncertainty across proteins; paired confidence intervals or bootstrap tests are needed.

Structure evaluation covers only 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. TPS evaluation also filters to low-confidence examples. These are meaningful targeted settings, but broader evaluation is needed to establish overall benefits and degradation rates. ESM3 training overlap with the historical CAMEO targets is also not addressed.

The perplexity argument does not explain why adaptation improves downstream performance. Lower reconstruction loss on the sequence being optimized can reflect memorization, and correlations on held-out sequences do not establish a causal benefit from minimizing that loss. Figure 11 itself shows fitness performance deteriorating while perplexity continues to decrease.

Efficiency and comparison evidence are incomplete. Matching the number of ESMFold predictions does not match total computation because TTT adds backward passes, and ESM3's eight-step decoding baseline is not matched to the TTT budget. The reported ESM3 runtime rises from roughly one second to twenty seconds. Broader latency and memory measurements, plus controlled comparisons of update strategies, would better establish practical value.

Some reproducibility and validation details remain unresolved. The TPS protocol does not clearly separate TTT hyperparameter selection from the folds used to report performance, code release is promised rather than supplied, and Figure 12's description of the selected configuration is ambiguous. The claimed preferential benefit for low-MSA-depth proteins is also not consistently supported by Table 5, where several larger gains occur at medium depth.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: improving predictions for an individual protein without additional experimental labels or homologous sequences. Adapting the backbone while retaining pretrained downstream modules is broadly applicable.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning structure, fitness, and function prediction across multiple architectures and model sizes. Table 1 shows improvements over both unadapted models and relevant inference baselines, including ESMFold masked prediction.

The fitness evaluation uses a separate MaveDB validation collection, excluding ProteinGym proteins by UniProt identifier. Five-seed experiments, documented hyperparameter searches, and explicit avoidance of ESMFold checkpoint leakage strengthen the evaluation.

The SAbDab experiments provide experimental-structure evidence beyond the small CAMEO benchmark: improvements occur for 115/175 antibody CDR structures and 487/814 antigen chains. Implementation examples and detailed appendices also support practical adoption.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the approach primarily combines established masked-language-model test-time training, SGD, LoRA, and confidence-based checkpoint selection. The contribution is principally empirical, requiring stronger evidence than currently provided for several headline claims.

The claim of improving 19% of BFVD structures is based on predicted pLDDT, which also selects the outputs. Correlation with agreement to high-confidence AlphaFold2 predictions is useful but does not establish accuracy on the low-confidence targets where AlphaFold2 fails. Cross-model confidence calibration and broader experimental-structure validation are needed; the reported percentage should be framed as confidence improvement.

The main structure benchmark contains only 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. This is a reasonable targeted setting, but does not establish general improvements or safety on unfiltered targets, particularly for other architectures. Seed variability does not quantify uncertainty across proteins, and the larger case studies omit the masked-prediction baseline.

Fitness improvements for the stronger models are small: 0.4139 to 0.4153 for ESM2-650M, 0.4569 to 0.4583 for SaProt-650M, and 0.5068 to 0.5087 for ProSST. The reported paired significance test is helpful, but comprehensive leaderboard comparisons and protein-level effect distributions are missing, leaving the broad state-of-the-art claim insufficiently established.

There is a material mismatch between the main method and several experiments. Table A3 states that most fitness experiments train on all tokens, including unmasked and special tokens, rather than only masked positions as in Equation 2. Appendix E.2.3 also updates the language-model head, which participates in fitness scoring, complicating the frozen-head claim. Controlled ablations should distinguish these variants and identify which changes produce the gains.

The perplexity argument is suggestive rather than explanatory: correlation across held-out proteins does not imply that fitting one sequence improves its downstream representation. Figure A10 actually shows continued perplexity reduction alongside deteriorating fitness performance. The efficiency claim also needs qualification: the reported ESMFold runtime increases from 2 to 46 seconds, while the AlphaFold2 comparison uses estimates rather than matched measurements.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: improving predictions for an individual protein without collecting additional labels or homologous sequences. The adaptation procedure is simple and applicable to several existing architectures.

There is concrete evidence of improved structure prediction. On the challenging CAMEO subset, ESMFold’s mean TM-score increases from 0.4649 to 0.5047, exceeding the masked-prediction baseline’s 0.4862. Improvements also transfer to ESM3 and HelixFold-Single.

The empirical coverage is substantial, spanning structure, fitness, and two function prediction tasks. The SAbDab experiments provide additional evidence against experimental structures, with improvements for 115 of 175 antibody CDR substructures and 487 of 814 antigen chains.

Several evaluation choices are careful: fitness hyperparameters are tuned on separate MaveDB proteins, ESMFold v0 is chosen to avoid CAMEO leakage, structure baselines include confidence-based candidate selection, and many results use five random seeds. The appendices provide extensive implementation and hyperparameter details.
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is primarily the transfer of established masked-modeling test-time training to proteins, combined with standard SGD, LoRA, and confidence-based checkpoint selection. This can be valuable, but the paper provides limited ablation evidence identifying which components are necessary or explaining when single-sequence adaptation helps.

The headline claim of improving 19% of BFVD structures exceeds the available accuracy evidence. The database-wide result measures increased pLDDT, which is also used to select adaptation checkpoints and compare different predictors. Agreement with high-confidence AlphaFold2 structures is useful corroboration, but does not establish accuracy on the difficult proteins where AlphaFold2 itself has low confidence. The one experimental example does not validate the database-wide claim.

The main structure benchmark contains only 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. This is a reasonable targeted setting, but leaves general performance and degradation on the remaining targets unresolved. Seed variability does not quantify uncertainty across proteins, and the SAbDab study lacks comparisons with specialized antibody predictors or the masked-prediction baseline.

Fitness gains for the stronger models are small: average Spearman increases by 0.0014 for both ESM2-650M and SaProt-650M, and by 0.0019 for ProSST. The reported paired significance test supports an improvement over ProSST, but the limited comparator set does not adequately establish the broader state-of-the-art claim. Function gains are also modest, with localization accuracy increasing from 0.627 to 0.634.

The implemented objective differs materially from the central presentation. Table A3 states that all five main fitness configurations train on every token, including unmasked and special tokens, whereas Equation 2 specifies loss only on selected masked positions. An ablation is needed to establish whether the advertised masked-reconstruction method or this alternative objective produces the reported gains.

The perplexity argument is suggestive rather than explanatory. A correlation between held-out perplexity and downstream accuracy does not establish that reducing training loss on one sequence improves its representation. Figure A10 itself shows regimes where perplexity decreases while fitness performance deteriorates. Likewise, Table A4 does not consistently support the claim that improvements are concentrated at low MSA depth.

The efficiency claim needs a more controlled comparison. Figure A4 measures approximately 46 seconds for ESMFold plus ProteinTTT versus 2 seconds for ESMFold, but estimates AlphaFold2 runtime from external ratios and assumed MSA-search costs. Direct measurements and accuracy-versus-compute comparisons would better substantiate practical advantages.

strengths: ProteinTTT offers a simple, practically useful way to adapt pretrained protein models to an individual target without requiring additional labeled data. Its compatibility with existing downstream heads makes the approach broadly applicable.

The empirical breadth is a substantial strength: experiments cover three structure predictors, multiple fitness predictors and model sizes, and two function prediction tasks. Improvements across these settings support the usefulness of per-protein adaptation beyond a single architecture.

Structure prediction gains are meaningful on the selected challenging targets. ESMFold’s mean TM-score increases from 0.4649 to 0.5047, exceeding the masked-prediction baseline at 0.4862. The SAbDab evaluation provides additional experimental-structure evidence, with improved LDDT for 115/175 antibody CDR structures and 487/814 antigen chains.

The evaluation includes several sound practices: a separate MaveDB validation collection for fitness hyperparameters, an ESMFold checkpoint chosen to avoid CAMEO training leakage, five-seed reporting, and a masked-prediction baseline with the same number of candidate predictions. Detailed implementation and hyperparameter descriptions aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is primarily the application of existing masked-modeling test-time training to proteins. SGD, LoRA, and confidence-based checkpoint selection are established components; the contribution rests mainly on empirical biological utility. The claim of being the first customization method in biological machine learning needs narrower positioning relative to existing protein-specific adaptation.

The main structure benchmark contains only 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets, selected using ESMFold confidence and ESM2 perplexity. This supports effectiveness on a particular difficult subset but does not establish broad structure-prediction improvements or safety on already accurate predictions. Target-level uncertainty, full-benchmark results, and compute-matched comparisons would strengthen the evidence.

The claim of improving 19% of BFVD structures principally measures higher predicted confidence, not experimentally verified accuracy. Selecting structures by maximum pLDDT also requires calibration across models and after adaptation. Agreement with high-confidence AlphaFold2 references is useful corroboration, but does not establish accuracy for the low-confidence AlphaFold2 cases motivating this experiment.

Fitness gains for the strongest models are small: ProSST improves from 0.5068 to 0.5087, and both 650M models improve by 0.0014. Function gains are similarly modest. The reported paired significance test is helpful, but seed variability does not capture uncertainty across proteins. Moreover, comparison against the selected baselines alone does not substantiate an unrestricted ProteinGym state-of-the-art claim.

There is a material discrepancy between the stated objective and several experiments. Table A3 says the principal fitness experiments propagate loss through all tokens, including unmasked and special tokens, whereas Equation (2) optimizes masked positions only. A direct ablation is needed to establish which objective drives the results. Appendix A also overstates the mechanistic justification: lower perplexity on the sequence being optimized does not imply better downstream representations, and Figure A10 shows downstream deterioration despite decreasing perplexity.

Efficiency claims need qualification. Figure A4 reports approximately 46 seconds for ESMFold plus ProteinTTT versus 2 seconds for ESMFold, while AlphaFold2 timings are estimates rather than matched measurements. The antibody study evaluates individual chains and CDR geometry, so its results should also be distinguished from accurate antibody–antigen complex or interaction prediction.
